title: Responsive Teaching Part 1, Learning is Recursive Not Linear
author: Carl Hendrick
summary: In the first of a series written while working with Australian schools implementing the AERO and VTLM models, Carl Hendrick lays out the principles behind responsive teaching. He contrasts the tidy linear model of curriculum and assessment, which he says serves accountability systems more than students, with the recursive way deep conceptual understanding actually develops. Using photosynthesis, proportionality and democracy as examples, he argues that students need to re-encounter ideas in new contexts, that misunderstandings surface after we assume learning has happened, and that progress often means refinement rather than accumulation. He defines responsive teaching as using evidence of student thinking before, during and after instruction to make deliberate adjustments, and links it to Shulman's pedagogical content knowledge. The second half catalogues 'lethal mutations': responsive teaching is not following every interest, not activity-led planning, not ability grouping, not mere questioning technique, not reactive teaching and not abandoning curriculum progression.
points: Hendrick argues linear curriculum models appeal to systems because they make accountability tidy, while meaningful learning meanders, loops back and sometimes stalls before accelerating.
He concedes some learning, such as letter sounds or arithmetic facts, is genuinely sequential, but says richer conceptual understanding emerges recursively.
Each re-encounter with a concept transforms prior understanding, so a student comes to know photosynthesis differently rather than simply knowing more.
Responsive teaching requires teachers to act as diagnosticians who know content in several ways, drawing on Shulman's pedagogical content knowledge.
He warns that 'lethal mutations', especially reactive teaching that bounces between student comments, masquerade as responsiveness while abandoning clear learning goals.
quotes: They promise that all students will arrive at the same destination at the same time. But learning is messy. It meanders, loops back, and crucially, it sometimes stalls before it accelerates.
Each encounter doesn't simply add new information, it transforms the understanding that came before. The student doesn't just know more about photosynthesis; they know it differently.

How often have we seen students appear to master a concept, only to reveal fundamental confusions when encountering it in a new context? The student who can solve quadratic equations algorithmically but cannot recognise a parabolic relationship in a real-world problem has learnt something, but not what we thought they had learnt.

Responsive teaching is an approach to instruction that prioritises ongoing assessment and adaptation. It means using evidence of student thinking, before, during, and after teaching to adjust instruction in real time.

Like many powerful educational ideas, responsive teaching has suffered from what we might call "lethal mutations”, well-intentioned misinterpretations that fundamentally alter its DNA. These mutations are particularly dangerous because they often masquerade as the real thing, leading to implementations that not only fail to improve learning but can actively undermine it.

Responsive teaching is not reactive teaching. Perhaps most importantly, responsive teaching is not simply reacting to whatever emerges in the moment without pedagogical purpose. Reactive teaching bounces from student comment to student comment without maintaining focus on learning goals.

These misconceptions often arise when responsive teaching is implemented as a collection of techniques rather than understood as a principled approach grounded in how learning actually works. The recursive nature of learning demands systematic responsiveness, not pedagogical permissiveness.
